Accessible Summary
What is known on the subject?
• In daily psychiatric practice, understanding individuals often involves formulating 
the clinical case, which may lead to viewing them solely as symptoms to be solved. 
Consequently, it can be challenging to see the individual beyond their symptoms. 
However, trying to understand the individual by his/her writings about narratives 
can offer broader perspectives and extend beyond being a medium for patients 
to express their experiences. On understanding writing, hermeneutics will be a 
resourceful method.

What the paper adds to existing knowledge?
• This study aims to propose a reevaluation of the nature of therapeutic communication among individuals with schizophrenia, psychiatrists, and psychiatric nurses 
by interpreting their writings on the same written narratives through a hermeneutic analysis. Our study has unique features compared to previous studies on 
communication between mental health professionals and patients. We directly 
investigated the act of understanding through the writings of the three groups of 
participants. The participants were also engaged in reading and writing about the 
narratives instead of relying on clinical interviews or self-report questionnaires. 
To the best of our knowledge, our study is the first hermeneutic study to examine 
the nature of reflection while all three groups encounter the same narratives as 
readers.
implications for practice?
• The results point to the need for psychiatrists/psychiatric nurses to develop new 
perspectives and skills in understanding/interacting with individuals with schizophrenia. Our study could be a pioneer sample in applying hermeneutics as a prevailing method to mental health nursing practice.

1  | INTRODUCTION
Although Philosophy of Communication and Psychiatry employ distinct theories and methodologies, both are concerned 
with the subject of communication. While the pioneer studies of 
contemporary philosophy (e.g. Blanchot, 1995; Deleuze, 1990; 
Deleuze & Guattari, 1993; Derrida, 1992, 1997) keep giving inspiration to the recent studies of philosophy of communication (e.g. 
Canar, 2024/2013, Chang & Butchard, 2012, Canar & Chang, 2018) 
in terms of emphasising the importance of thinking through writing 
itself and using literature as a fundamental reference for communication studies, this viewpoint finds limited space within the field of 
psychiatry.
In psychiatry, understanding the phenomenological basis 
of the patient's experience becomes crucial (O'yebode, 2015). 
Understanding the illness phenomenon from the individual's point 
of view ensures more sensitive treatment and care plans, improves

therapeutic alliance and adherence to treatment, increases quality of care and satisfaction with the care (Cooper et al., 2013; 
McCabe, 2013; Moreno-Poyato, 2021). In line with Rollo May's 
emphasis on understanding (May, 1994; May et al., 1958), there 
can be various ways to understand the individual and especially in 
psychiatry diversifying ways of understanding can create a better 
care provision experience for both the individual and health professional. The concept of writing could be viewed as a means of facilitating understanding rather than a technique. Within the context 
of psychiatry, writing serves as a medium through which patients 
can express themselves. This utilisation of writing as a therapeutic 
tool is particularly evident in approaches such as ‘expressive writing’ (Baikie & Wilhelm, 2005) or ‘written exposure therapy’ (Sloan & 
Marx, 2019). In daily psychiatric practice, understanding individuals 
often involves formulating the clinical case, which may lead to viewing them solely as symptoms to be solved. Consequently, it can be 
challenging to see the individual beyond their symptoms. However, 
Abstract
Introduction: Understanding individuals with schizophrenia is an essential but challenging phenomenon in psychiatry.
Aim/Question: This study proposes a reevaluation of the nature of therapeutic communication among individuals with schizophrenia, psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses 
by interpreting their writings on the same written narratives through a hermeneutic 
analysis.
Method: In this study, employing a qualitative descriptive methodology utilising hermeneutic analysis, participants read the five narratives, wrote down their opinions on 
each narratives and answered nine questions to express their own personal writing 
experiences.
Results: Participants from each group acted as both ‘readers’ and ‘authors’ while 
rewriting the selected five short narratives based on their own sense of readings. 
The expression, rewriting refers to the act of reading and written interpretations 
of participants and researchers in this study. While individuals with schizophrenia primarily focused on the text (narrative) in their readings and writings, psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses tended to focus on reader (themselves) in their 
interpretations.

Discussion: Although reading should be approached as a process of discovery 
rather than merely seeking predetermined knowledge, psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses read the narratives as if the author were a patient or as the signs of an 
illness.
Implications for Practice: The results point to the need for psychiatrists/psychiatric 
nurses to develop new perspectives and skills in understanding and interacting with 
individuals with schizophrenia.
KEYWORDS
hermeneutics, interpretation, philosophy of communication, psychiatric nursing, psychiatry, 
psychosis, writing
   CANAR et al. |  183
trying to understand the individual by his/her writings on narratives 
can offer broader perspectives and extend beyond being a medium 
for patients to express their experiences.
The fact that writing can be used as an alternative means of 
understanding an individual, makes understanding and interpreting what is written an important issue. On understanding writing, hermeneutics known as ‘the science or art of interpretation’ 
(Grondin, 1994, p. 1), will be a resourceful method. Hermeneutics 
involves understanding the meaning of specific experiences by considering the contextual factors in which they arise. Trying to understand what is going on in the world of individuals with schizophrenia 
from the perspective of individuals and healthcare professionals can 
not only broaden our perspective on understanding patients better, 
but also help us to see how health professionals understand the patient's world and experience of illness.
Schizophrenia is a disorder that is difficult to understand for people living with it, their relatives and health professionals, and people 
with schizophrenia feel that they are not well understood (Gaebel 
& Salveridou-Hof, 2022; Kelly & Buchanan, 2022; Pérez-Álvarez 
et al., 2016). Therefore, our study specifically includes individuals 
with schizophrenia to explore how writing experiences can illuminate their thought processes and narrative interpretation rather 
than specifically discussing their own experiences. The perspectives 
of psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses in their reading of these selected narratives are also crucial to this study, as it explores their 
reactions when faced with a text instead of a patient during the act 
of reading (understanding).

Our study has unique features compared to previous studies 
on understanding patients and mental health professionals. We 
directly investigated the act of understanding within the three 
groups of participants. The participants were also engaged in 
reading and writing about the narratives instead of relying on clinical interviews or self-report questionnaires. This distinguishes our 
study from previous research, which often focused on exploring 
the meaning of specific concepts, such as decision-making, or the 
experience of communication, making it difficult to separate from 
a clinical task (O'Brien, 2000). To the best of our knowledge, our 
study is the first hermeneutic study to examine the nature of reflection while all three groups encounter the same narratives as 
readers.
This study aimed to perform a hermeneutic analysis of the 
writings of individuals with schizophrenia, psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses on the selected narratives in order to compare their 
process of understanding and reflection on the same narratives. 
Understanding, interpretation and application are what hermeneutics involve for Hans-Georg Gadamer (Lawn & Keane, 2011, p. 
11). However, hermeneutic analysis is often perceived as a method 
that is challenging to apply in practice. This perception arises from 
the fact that studies on hermeneutics predominantly concentrate 
on theoretical aspects of interpretation rather than its practical 
application. Even Gadamer's ‘own interests concern the application of hermeneutics to education, history, medical science and 
literature’ (Lawn & Keane, 2011, p. 11) his studies basically reflect 
hermeneutics as a Gadamerian theory. In addition, ‘because of the 
universal application of the interpretative process, every phenomenon falls within the scope of hermeneutics. Nevertheless, each 
aspect of interpretation has its own area of application and specific region of concern’ (Lawn & Keane, 2011, p. 11). Gadamer's 
hermeneutics is practical to underline how our application of 
hermeneutics might be different since ‘for Gadamer (…) the real

challenge is to accept and comprehend that the inherent structure of all understanding is (…) always-understanding- differently’ 
(as cited in Brockmeier & Meretoja, 2014, p. 5). In short, different 
understandings give rise to different methodologies to interpret. 
Since each interpretation is various and diversified in its own 
sense, Gadamer's philosophy would not be strictly followed in applying hermeneutics in this study.
In this study, individuals with schizophrenia, psychiatrists and 
psychiatric nurses were given the same narratives and asked to 
write their views on these narratives, which were then interpreted 
through hermeneutic analysis. It is hoped that this methodology 
will serve as a mirror for how patients and health professionals 
who are exposed to the same narratives interpret them. The methodology used in this study will provide highly objective feedback 
on how we as health professionals are doing in understanding patients by showing the differences between us and patients on how 
we interpret those situations when we are exposed to the same 
situations.
2  | METHODS
2.1  |  Design
This study utilised a qualitative descriptive research design. The 
focus of the study was on the utilisation of hermeneutics throughout various phases of a research project, including preparation, 
conducting the research and analysing the results. We particularly 
emphasised the interpretation of participants' experiences as conveyed through their written narratives. By adopting this approach, 
writing serves a purpose beyond being a mere means of expressing the unspeakable, unnamable or inexpressible for participants. 
Instead, it becomes a space of thinking enabling participants to perceive themselves as readers and thinkers, thereby expanding their 
self-awareness and understanding. Secondly, multidisciplinary view 
in this study, encompassing philosophy of communication, psychiatry and psychiatric nursing, offers a new perspective for applying hermeneutics. Thirdly, despite the three distinct participant 
groups—individuals with schizophrenia, psychiatrists and psychiatric 
nurses—we assigned their roles in parenthesis. This approach allowed all participants to engage as both readers and writers of selected narratives, providing an opportunity for them to express their

thoughts and reflections on texts. Finally, examining how readers 
engage with selected texts can contribute to reconsidering the interaction between individuals with schizophrenia, psychiatrists and 
psychiatric nurses. By recognising that reading, in its broader sense, 
184 |    CANAR et al.
plays a significant role in defining who we are (Manguel, 2010), this 
study offers insights into the dynamics and relationships within 
these groups.
2.2  |  Setting and participants
This study was conducted in Ankara, Türkiye, encompassing two university hospitals and one community mental health centre (CMHC). 
The CMHC provided drug compliance follow-ups and offered diverse occupational activities. The study involved three participant 
groups: individuals with schizophrenia (n= 10), psychiatrists (n= 16) 
and psychiatric nurses (n= 15). Participants with schizophrenia were 
outpatients in remission.
The psychiatrists and the psychiatric nurses were employed 
in the two hospitals as well as in the CMHC. The detailed information on descriptive features of the participants is presented in 
Appendix S1.
The inclusion criteria for individuals with schizophrenia were 
(1) meeting DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013) diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia, (2) having a minimum education 
of 5 years, (3) scoring <70 on Positive and Negative Symptom Scale 
(Kay et al., 1987; Kostakoğlu et al., 1999), (4) maintaining consistent 
medication for the last 6 months, (5) scoring <2 on all items of the 
Thought and Language Disorder Scale (Kircher et al., 2014; Mutlu 
et al., 2019). The last three criteria defined the remission period of 
the disorder and for the identification of obvious formal thought disorder. These criteria were necessary, as the study aimed to investigate the patient's writings and readings, rather than the symptoms 
of the disorder.
The exclusion criteria for the schizophrenia group were (1) 
meeting DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013) diagnostic criteria of any psychiatric disorder other than schizophrenia, (2)

having medical conditions hindering data collection. The Positive 
and Negative Symptom Scale (PANSS) is a 30-item scale utilised to 
evaluate the three symptom dimensions of schizophrenia: positive, 
negative and general psychopathology. Rating is based on clinical 
observation and collateral information obtained through a semistructured interview. In this study, PANSS was employed to assess 
the clinical status and severity of symptoms in the patients. The 
Thought and Language Disorder Scale is a 30-item semi-structured 
scale that enables a comprehensive examination of formal thought 
disorders.
The inclusion criteria for psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses 
were as follows: (1) being <65 years of age, (2) not having serious 
medical or neurological conditions that could hinder the process 
of responding to data collection tools. Convenience sampling was 
employed to select participants for the study, including (1) individuals with schizophrenia, (2) psychiatrists and (3) psychiatric nurses. 
Initially, it was planned to include 20 individuals in each group, totalling 60 participants. However, due to COVID-19 curfews in Türkiye, 
the recruitment period had to be halted after reaching 41 participants. Participants meeting the inclusion criteria were invited to join 
the study, informed about the study's aims and methods, and subsequently, individual interviews were conducted. The study included 
10 individuals with schizophrenia, 16 psychiatrists and 15 psychiatric nurses who volunteered. No withdrawals occurred during any 
phase of the study.
2.3  |  Data collection/ procedure
Among the researchers, two were faculty members from Faculty 
of Communication and the Faculty of Nursing at a state university. 
Additionally, two researchers were psychiatrists working at a CMHC 
and a university hospital. The researchers had prior experience conducting qualitative studies and had actively participated in various 
courses, training programs and workshops related to the subject 
matter.
Written consent for participation was obtained. Subsequently, 
participants were escorted to a secluded and secure room where 
they completed a sociodemographic form. They were then instructed to read and express their opinions on five narratives 
(Non-Existent Man, The Street Lamp, Runner from the Sun, Nocturnal

Patrol at the Orchestra Saloon and Paradox, Appendix S2) on The 
Narrative Form (Appendix S3). Following their written opinions 
on the narratives, participants were provided with The Evaluation 
Form (Appendix S4) to express their opinions. The initial interviews and administration of data collection tools were conducted 
by Author 4 and Author 3 for psychiatrists and individuals with 
schizophrenia. Author 2 conducted the initial interviews and data 
collection specifically with psychiatric nurses. Each participant 
was represented by a letter and number including A for individuals 
with schizophrenia, B psychiatrists and C for psychiatric nurses 
and numbers for participants were assigned randomly (i.e. A1, B8, 
C15).
Sociodemographic and clinical characteristics were obtained 
using a sociodemographic form developed by the researchers 
Author 1 and Author 2. The Narrative Form consisted of the narratives written by Author 1 along with a corresponding question for 
each narrative. The selection of the narratives was based on two 
criteria. The first was that the participants had not read these narratives before as reading the narratives for the first time and then 
writing about them was crucial for this study. Although Author 
1's selected narratives were all published previously, none of the 
participants could come across those narratives before since they 
were not widespread publications (Appendix S3) The second criterion was the plot, and the writing style of each narrative should 
be abstract, thought-provoking and unusual (Appendix S3) since a 
challenging text always provokes various interpretations. Author 
1 chose five narratives of her among the other narratives which 
match with these criteria. The Evaluation Form drawing from the 
researchers' expertise in communication sciences, psychiatry 
and psychiatric nursing, was jointly created by Author 1, Author 
2, Author 3 and Author 4. The form consisted of nine questions 
in total. To examine the comprehensibility of the forms, drafts 
   CANAR et al. |  185
were administered to an individual with schizophrenia, a psychiatrist and a psychiatric nurse. It was found that the respondents 
correctly understood the questions, leading to no revisions being 
necessary for the forms.

The entire recruitment and data collection process lasted approximately 100 min, which included a 10-min break for individuals 
with schizophrenia. For psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses, the 
process took approximately 40–50 min. Data collection was conducted over a period spanning from January 2020 to December 
2021.
2.4  |  Data analysis
This study is an analysis of participants' writings on five short 
narratives based on hermeneutics. Hermeneutics emphasises the 
importance of understanding texts without relying on personal 
opinions or biases (Gadamer, 2006; Simms, 2016). During three 
sessions, the researchers engaged in discussions regarding the potential primary categories. Drawing from Gadamer's insights into 
hermeneutics, the concept of text was considered as a hermeneutical concept in this study. As a result, ‘text’ was identified as one 
of the three key categories used for interpreting the participants' 
writings. The second category identified in the study is ‘author’, 
and the final category, equally important, is ‘reader’. Throughout 
the study, the categories of text, author and reader were interchangeable, assuming different roles at different stages. To signify 
the interchangeable nature of the main categories, stages were 
established and presented in Table 1.
During the first stage, the primary focus was on participants' 
writings. Neither the text, the style of the writing nor the author as 
a personage was taken into consideration to interpret participants' 
writings. In this stage, researchers themselves were also considered as readers, rather than interpreters of the author or the texts. 
Participants (readers) engaged in reading the texts, while researchers (also readers) focused on reading the participants themselves to 
comprehend (interpret) their writings. The text became the reader on 
the first stage.
In the second stage, text became participants' writings on selected narratives. The roles of author and reader transitioned to the 
researchers who acted as rewriters. During the first stage, participants also engaged in rewriting by reading and writing about the

narratives, although their process aimed at understanding the narratives rather than analysing them. The researchers read participants' 
writings for interpretation. The concept of the author no longer represented the original narrative author or participants but referred to 
the researchers themselves.
In the third stage, the participants' responses in the Evaluation 
Form became the text, as these answers in the text formed a new 
(different) text. Participants became author while researchers became readers. The focus shifted from the original writings on the 
narratives to the ‘interpretation of the interpretation’ facilitated 
by selected questions. Participants' answers in the Evaluation Form
helped researchers to make a comprehensive interpretation to reveal a new understanding. To ensure reflexivity, the researchers 
consistently questioned and discussed their own positions, feelings, 
thoughts and assumptions regarding the research process throughout the analysis phase. Throughout and following the study process, 
the researchers maintained equal power dynamics, which fostered 
an environment where participants could freely express their opinions without experiencing any pressure or anxiety. This contributed 
to the trustworthiness of the data collected. The researchers individually analysed and interpreted the data, employing investigator 
triangulation, which further enhanced the credibility of the study 
(Patton, 2014). For transferability, our study clearly outlined the 
study setting, participants, sampling method, characteristics of the 
participants, inclusion criteria, data collection procedure, as well 
as the narratives and forms used in settings and participants, data 
collection and data analysis sections. To ensure confirmability and 
dependability, the researchers organised multiple meetings to discuss interpretations, refine the analysis and establish consensus on 
categories. The data analysis process was thoroughly described, enhancing the transparency and replicability of the study.
2.5  |  Ethical considerations
The study protocol received approval from the Hacettepe University 
Noninvasive Research Ethics Committee (project number: GO 
19/715).
3  |  RESULTS
The study involved three main categories: text, author and reader, 
which were further divided into three stages (Table 1). In the first 
stage, the category of text referred to selected narratives. In the

second stage, the category of text represented the writings of

186 |    CANAR et al.
participants (the results of participants' readings). Despite the 
brevity of five narratives, participants found reading and providing their thoughts on these texts to be a challenging task. In the 
second stage, the participants' writings were further categorised 
into sub-categories, which aligned with the main categories of 
text, author and reader. Third stage was participants' responses 
in the evaluation form. Although participants filled the evaluation 
form to reveal how this experience of writing was for them, their 
answers also revealed their own method of reading. As evaluation 
form became another text to be studied, we defined it as a third 
stage of the text (Table 1).
The second main category in this study was the Author. The term 
‘author’ encompassed various roles throughout different stages, including the author of selected narratives, researchers and participants themselves. In participants' writings, the author could refer to 
either ‘a patient’ or ‘an amateur’.
Engaging in the process of understanding and writing about the 
texts acted as a form of self-defence, particularly for psychiatrists 
and psychiatric nurses, as they grappled with the meanings embedded within the narratives.
If the readers struggled to comprehend the text, it was often attributed to the dispersion of ideas/language, the perception of the 
author as an individual with schizophrenia, or the assumption that 
the author lacked proficient writing skills due to being an amateur. 
The writing style itself posed as one of the reasons for the difficulty 
of reading (understanding) these texts. As the participants were unfamiliar with the author's identity, they found it necessary to ‘create

the author’ (to construct a mental image of the author) in order to 
make sense of the written material. Excerpts from writings of participants are presented in Appendix S5.
Participants occasionally assumed the role of the author, offering 
advice on writing techniques or disregarding the author altogether 
to focus solely on their own interpretation of the text. Despite their 
attempts to concentrate on their personal reading experience, they 
emphasised the necessity of knowing the author's identity to enhance the readability and understanding of the text. The researchers' hermeneutic analysis involved not only reading the texts but 
also considering each reading as an opportunity for reinterpretation 
and rewriting (Table 1).
Reader was the third category. In our study, we examined how 
readers (researchers) read other readers (participants) and analysed the similarities and differences in their reading experiences. 
Psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses identified themselves primarily 
as readers, whereas individuals with schizophrenia considered themselves akin to the unknown author, focusing on the text rather than 
the act of reading when expressing their thoughts (Table 1).
The writings produced by individuals with schizophrenia were 
categorised within category of ‘text’. These individuals approached 
each narrative as a contemplation, they enjoyed what they were 
reading. Their engagement with narratives was based on understanding the anonymous author. Rather than assuming the author's 
voice, they found solace and enjoyment in the company of the author as they engaged with the text. The task of reading and writing 
about the five narratives was generally challenging for psychiatrists 
and psychiatric nurses, as the narratives were typically perceived as 
highly abstract. Individuals with schizophrenia, as participants, provided concise and direct interpretations, displaying a strong sense of 
certainty regarding the meaning of the narratives. However, it is important to acknowledge that there were exceptions that surpassed 
the boundaries of generalisation.
Individuals with schizophrenia directed their attention towards 
the text itself. When asked about their thoughts on Non-Existent 
Man, their responses indicated that they did not find the character 
to be strange or peculiar. Instead, they centred their understanding 
on the main non-character of the narrative. They literally understood

the situation and accepted him as he was (Appendix S5).
A concise overview of how each individual with schizophrenia 
interpreted the narratives is shown in Table 2.
Psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses approached their writings 
on the five narratives from the perspective of the reader category. 
They often viewed each narrative as a form of speech originating 
from an individual with a mental illness. Their writings became 
answering to a patient or speak in the name of the author, who is 
probably a patient. Psychiatrists displayed a reluctance to engage in 
diagnostic practices while reading a short narrative. Nevertheless, 
their approach to reading appeared to involve gathering symptoms, 
and ultimately making a diagnosis. In this context, the role of the 
reader for psychiatrists was primarily that of an observer in their 
writings (Appendix S5).
The question, ‘what do you think about the narrative’ is taken 
as ‘what the narrative is about’ for psychiatrists. In cases where a 
narrative posed challenges for them, they resorted to providing a 
summary of the story instead. If summarising proved difficult, they 
shifted their focus to the author's writing style (Appendix S5).
Additionally, specific words or expressions have been highlighted 
in bold letters in Table 3 to emphasise the defining characteristics of 
psychiatrists' readings.
In contrast to psychiatrists, the role of the reader for psychiatric 
nurses appeared different. Their approach to reading the narratives

seemed to involve seeking ‘the correct answer’ initially, suggesting 
a focus on finding the most accurate interpretation or response. 
Psychiatric nurses' interpretations surpassed simple questionanswering, showcasing greater diversity compared to psychiatrists. 
Their comments as readers displayed distinctiveness and lacked 
resemblance to each other (Appendix S5). The summary of nurses' 
writings can be read in Table 4.
Based on the sociodemographic form, it was found that a majority of individuals with schizophrenia expressed their fondness for 
reading and their ability to recall the books they had recently read. 
On the other hand, the psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses predominantly expressed a greater interest in writing rather than reading 
(Appendix S1).
The Evaluation Form in Appendix S4 provides insights into the 
participants' personal writing experiences. Individuals with schizophrenia felt more comfortable and defined this writing process as 
‘interesting’ (i.e. A10), ‘happy’ (i.e. A2) and ‘gaining an experience’ (i.e. 
A1) while psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses defined this experience 
as ‘difficult’ as if they were in a difficult exam (i.e. B8, B15, C10, C3).
The text, Paradox proved to be the most challenging for nearly all 
participants in terms of comprehension. When attempting to identify the main ideas (central themes), individuals with schizophrenia 
had various guesses. Psychiatrists typically emphasised the lack of 
central themes, as the abstractness of narratives did not provide 
much insight. Psychiatric nurses suggested that central themes 
were connected to ‘inner world’ and ‘psychotic disorders of patients’ 
(Appendix S4).
Individuals with schizophrenia did not pay much attention 
whether these narratives were connected with each other or not, 
while psychiatric nurses underlined that all of them were connected 
as they were the writings of patients. Psychiatrists, however, did not 
focus on that connection much (Appendix S4).
The responses of individuals with schizophrenia to the question, 
‘who is speaking in the texts’ portrayed the psychiatrist as an author, 
as if this was a sort of play. Psychiatrists firmly believed that the

patient, who was the author of these texts, was speaking. For psychiatric nurses, an ‘observer’ was speaking in these texts.
The following question aimed to determine the importance of 
knowing who was speaking in the texts. Only half of the participants 
with schizophrenia believed that it was important to know who was 
speaking in the text. The responses from psychiatrists could be interpreted in terms of how they needed to create the author, even in 
the absence of any clues. If only they could know who the author 
was, the text would have become more understandable. However, 
psychiatric nurses usually did not pay much attention and did not 
think it was important to know who was speaking in these texts 
(Appendix S4).
The question of what participants wanted to change in these 
narratives was noteworthy, as their responses reflected their rewritings of these narratives. Individuals with schizophrenia expressed a

4  | DISCUSSION
This study focuses on reading and interpretation experiences of 
individuals with schizophrenia, psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses 
through their own act of writings/personal engagements with the 
selected narratives. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first 
hermeneutic study to examine the nature of reflection while all 
three groups encounter the same narratives as readers. The participants (readers) in our study engage in a profound discussion that 
encompasses various perspectives on schizophrenia, mental illness, 
care/treatment and communication.
In this study, imagination is perceived as being akin to a manifestation of hallucination. Despite narratives typically being regarded as works of fiction, participants did not take five narratives 
as an instance of literature. As each narrative blurred the difference 
between real and fictitious, the author became an individual with 
schizophrenia while readers (participants) were taking the text as a 
declaration of his/her illness. In the realm of psychiatry, the focus is 
on individuals who require assistance and support. This is precisely

why the author should be a patient, as opposed to just anyone, for 
the psychiatrists involved in the study. Nonetheless, literature on 
reading and hermeneutics underscore the importance of avoiding 
superficial readings, urging deeper engagement with the text.
The interpretations primarily revolved around the potential purpose of this study for psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses. Once 
participants believed they had an answer to this question, their willingness to engage in the research and contribute through writing 
increased.
Three main categories—text, author and reader—were interchangeable with one another. The act of reading defined narratives 
in terms of these three categories. The reading experience varied 
for each participant depending on which category was pivotal. In 
this study, as participants with schizophrenia primarily focused 
on the text, their writings can be understood through the lens of 
Roland Barthes' notable statement regarding the death of the author 
(Barthes, 1977).
The way individuals with schizophrenia interacted with the text 
also aligns closely with Alberto Manguel's diverse definitions of 
‘ideal reader’ (Manguel, 2010). The concept of ideal reader helped 
in emphasising the text as a contemplation. It is worth noting that 
not every definition of the ideal reader was applicable to individuals 
with schizophrenia. However, when it came to aspects such as ‘intuition’ (i.e. A3), ‘enjoyment’ (i.e. A6, A8) and ‘participation’ (i.e. A7, 
A10), they all became ideal readers when they focused on the text 
(Manguel, 2010).
When it comes to expressing their enjoyment of reading, some 
psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses' readings align with Manguel's 
passion of reading. However, their acts of writing, are more like 
finding the correct answer to a question. In this case, the question 
revolves around the abstract narrative and providing an answer becomes akin to solving a problem.
The author of five narratives is anonymous, unknown for all 
participants. This study does not take the author's opinion as the 
correct meaning of the narratives into consideration. This anonymity helps us to give narratives (text) a priority. Participants

must create the author and transform him/her into a patient who 
is inexperienced in writing narratives to overcome the abstractness of the narratives. In Plato's Phaedrus, as cited by Ong, it is

noted that ‘… a written text is basically unresponsive. If you ask 
a person to explain his or her statement, you can get an explanation; if you ask a text, you get back nothing except the same, 
often stupid words which called for your question in the first 
place’ (Ong, 2002, p. 78). That is why the interpretation meant 
to speak in the name of the text, the author and the reader for 
participants. Since hermeneutics is involved with understanding, 
there was a need to figure out the peculiarities of each reading. 
Although participants' hermeneutics or ‘the science or art of interpretation’ (Grondin, 1994) were basically based on their hesitations about the writing style of the narratives and the purpose of 
reading them. Engaging in reading, participants sought to identify 
resemblances and discrepancies between the narratives and their 
own experiences. If they thought the narrative gave some answers 
to them, then the narrative made sense.

According to Alberto Manguel's notion of the ‘reader as a traveller’ (Manguel, 2013), as ‘reading is a traveling through the text’ 
(Manguel, 2013), our hermeneutic analysis is basically a travelling 
through participants' readings (writings). The focus is on demonstrating how reading, as an act, becomes a hermeneutic analysis in its 
own multidisciplinary sense.
Our analysis aims to reveal the intricacies of the reading process, functioning as a means to convey to readers the multifaceted 
nature of this interpretive journey. Currently, limited research has 
been conducted on the interpretations of both mental health professionals and individuals with mental health problems regarding 
the same experience. Schneider et al. (2004) examined communication dynamics between healthcare professionals and individuals 
diagnosed with schizophrenia and found a notable divergence between the experiences of patients and the viewpoints of healthcare 
professionals in terms of explaining the diagnosis providing information about the disorder and treatment. Wesseldijk-Elferink et al. 
described the experiences of patients with psychotic disorders and 
mental health nurses on the concept of shared-decision making 
(Wesseldijk-Elferink et al., 2021). They emphasised that patients feel 
ignored during the decision-making. To gain mutual understanding, 
our findings revealed that healthcare professionals' attitudes should 
get beyond a theoretical analysis of patients and should extend to 
focus on the experience of schizophrenia.
Our study has unique features compared to previous studies on 
communication between mental health professionals and patients. 
We directly investigated the act of understanding within the three 
groups of participants. We used hermeneutic analysis to attain this 
purpose. Hermeneutic analysis is focused on interpretation and 
understanding of human experience as it is lived. ‘What people 
say and do and why’ are the main questions guiding this methodology (Alsaigh & Coyne, 2021). This methodology unveils details to 
make the experience clear, with a purpose of generating meaning 
and reaching a sense of understanding (Kafle, 2013). It is used to

produce rich textual descriptions of the experience of a phenomenon where a deeper understanding of the meaning is looked for, 
through progressively layered reflection while using rich descriptive language (Kafle, 2013). Another important aspect of our study 
is that the participants were engaged in reading and writing about 
the narratives instead of relying on clinical interviews or self-report 
questionnaires. This distinguishes our study from previous research, 
which often focused on exploring the meaning of specific concepts, 
such as decision-making, or the experience of communication, making it difficult to separate from a clinical task (O'Brien, 2000).
4.1  |  Limitations
The participants' reliance on a reading method that emphasises a 
single correct meaning, which they were accustomed to, may have 
limited their interpretation of the texts. This sentiment was directly 
conveyed in the evaluation forms, where participants used expressions such as ‘I felt like I was in the exam’, ‘It made me feel like I was 
in high school’. In addition, their dislike of reading and writing may 
have posed difficulties during the writing process. Particularly, unwillingness of psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses to engage in reading and writing may have introduced certain limitations to the study. 
In addition, despite researchers' efforts to provide a quiet space for 
writing, the fact that participants had to read and express their opinions on five narratives within a clinical or hospital atmosphere could 
have affected their writings.
5  |  CONCLUSION
This hermeneutic analysis revealed that psychiatrists and psychiatric 
nurses read the narratives in terms of the sign of the unidentified 
author's monologue on his/her illness while individuals with schizophrenia understood the author to be potentially relatable to their 
own experiences, fostering a sense of connection.
Reading was mainly grasped in terms of ‘trying to understand 
what is going on in the text’ that was why the question, ‘what do 
you think about the narrative’, as willingly misunderstood as ‘what 
the narrative is about’.
The author was interpreted in terms of reading author's intentions of writing these narratives. In order to cope with the problem 
of the unknown author either they create the author or forget the

author. However, these efforts ultimately heightened the perception 
of the text's unreadability.
Reader was grasped in terms of being close or distant to the narrative. When adopting a distant stance, participants' interpretations 
focused on summarising the narrative. However, when they took a 
closer look at the text, they made connections between their own 
experiences and specific circumstances presented in the narratives. 
Participants offered writing advice, corrected ideas and emphasised the challenges of writing/interpreting rather than sharing their 
thoughts on the narratives.
The writings of individuals with schizophrenia, when not explicitly focused on themselves, cannot be labelled as examples of 
schizophrenic thinking. This study advocates for viewing individuals with schizophrenia as individuals rather than solely patients. The 
190 |    CANAR et al.
study's findings highlighted the importance for psychiatrists and 
psychiatric nurses to temporarily set aside their specialist roles when 
engaging with patients. It revealed that reading (interpreting) should 
be approached as a process of discovery rather than merely seeking 
predetermined knowledge.
Conversation between psychiatrists/psychiatric nurses and patients can indeed be viewed as a mutual process of discovery. This 
perspective acknowledges that the role of a psychiatrist/psychiatric nurse may not always be useful in deciphering or understanding 
creative writing (narratives) since such writings are works of fiction 
rather than hallucinations.
6  |  RELEVANCE STATEMENT
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first hermeneutic study 
to examine the nature of reflection while all three groups encounter the same narratives as readers. Based on the findings, 
individuals with schizophrenia primarily focus on the text (narrative) while psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses tend to focus on 
reader (themselves) in their interpretations. This study could be 
a reference for further researches that are based on a qualitative 
descriptive methodology utilising hermeneutic analysis. The narratives can also be used as samples for similar studies that focus 
on applying hermeneutics as a prevailing method to mental health 
nursing practice.
